title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes §20 and gives §§21–23 of E593. The whole paper serves one goal: turning a series of reciprocals into a continued fraction by means of the identity 1/s = α + α²/(−α + 1/t), where t is the tail of the series.

§20 (end). The integral s = ∫_0^1 x^{m-1}dx/(1+x^n) equals 1/m − 1/(m+n) + 1/(m+2n) − …. Putting α=m, β=m+n, … into the Theorem I fraction gives the partial denominators β−α = n, γ−β = n, …. So 1/s = m + m²/(n + (m+n)²/(n + (m+2n)²/(n + …))). Euler says he already gave this in Comm. Acad. Petrop. (old series) tom. XI, which is E123, 'De fractionibus continuis observationes'.

§21. For a series of positive terms s = Σ 1/α_k, replace β, δ, ζ, … by their negatives. This gives 1/s = α + α²/(−β−α + β²/(γ+β + γ²/(−δ−γ + …))). An equivalence transformation then changes the sign of every second partial denominator together with the adjacent numerator. The result is 1/s = α − α²/(α+β − β²/(β+γ − γ²/(γ+δ − …))). This is the classical 'Euler continued fraction formula' for a series, here in the form for reciprocals of the terms.

§22. Take α=ab, β=bc, γ=cd, δ=de, …, so that s = 1/(ab) − 1/(bc) + 1/(cd) − …. Theorem I gives 1/s = ab + a²b²/(b(c−a) + b²c²/(c(d−b) + c²d²/(d(e−c) + …))). Dividing each partial denominator by its common factor (b, c, d, …) and adjusting the numerators gives 1/s = ab + a²b/(c−a + bc/(d−b + cd/(e−c + …))). Dividing by a gives 1/(as) = b + ab/(c−a + bc/(d−b + cd/(e−c + …))).

§23 (Theorem II). If s = 1/(ab) − 1/(bc) + 1/(cd) − 1/(de) + 1/(ef) − …, then 1/(as) = b + ab/(c−a + bc/(d−b + cd/(e−c + de/(f−d + …)))).

The next page applies this. Adding a series to its shifted copy turns alternating sums like log 2 and π/4 into series with products of consecutive denominators. This yields fractions such as 1/(2 log2 − 1) = 2 + 1·2/(2 + 2·3/(2 + …)) and 4/(π−2) = 3 + 1·3/(4 + 3·5/(4 + …)).
errors: No mathematical errors. The equivalence transformations in §21 and §22 check out step by step: the sign changes in §21 and the division of each partial denominator by b, c, d, … in §22 are correct.

Formal caveat: the passage from the series to the infinite continued fraction is done termwise, with no discussion of convergence. This is typical for Euler and harmless here, since the continued fraction's approximants equal the series' partial sums.

ideas.modern_name: Euler's continued fraction for alternating series of reciprocals (Brouncker-type fraction, generalised)
ideas.where_published: E123, Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 11 (cited by Euler on this page); also Introductio (E101) ch. 18

ideas.what: Positive-term series Σ1/α_k turned into 1/s = α − α²/(α+β − β²/(β+γ − …)) by sign change and an equivalence transformation
ideas.modern_name: Euler's continued fraction formula (series ↔ continued fraction, with approximants equal to partial sums); equivalence transformation
ideas.where_published: Introductio in analysin infinitorum (E101), ch. 18; E123

ideas.where_published: This paper E593 (Nova Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 2, 1784/1788)

deep.surprise_reason: Every result on the page is a direct, correct specialisation of Euler's own well-known series-to-continued-fraction formula, already published in E101/E123 and in this printed paper. Nothing here appears unexploited or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: The print reads 'Comentar.' (single m) and 'Vet.', meaning Commentarii, old series, tom. XI. The transcription is fine; the reference is E123.
In §21 the scan reads 'loco litterarum β, δ, ζ, θ, scribatur −β, −δ, −ζ, etc.' The letter list seems to include θ, which is consistent with the transcription.
Page header numbers are ')160(' and ')161(', running heads of the original; the machine transcription has them right.
